In the morning, look at the layers on the bottom, with the heaviest bits lowest and fine mud on top. Rivers drop their mud the same way when they slow down, building flat plains year after year.

Glacier melt starts the river and keeps it flowing in the dry months, but most of the water in the Ganga comes from monsoon rain falling across its huge basin, along with the many rivers that join it.

sec.t:
High in [[@uttarakhand|Uttarakhand]], about 4,000 m up, meltwater pours out from under the snout of the Gangotri glacier. The opening is called Gaumukh, meaning "cow's mouth". The stream that rushes out is the Bhagirathi, named after a king who, in Hindu tradition, prayed to bring the goddess Ganga down from the heavens to Earth.

The Bhagirathi tumbles down steep [[@valleys|valleys]]. At Devprayag, it meets the Alaknanda, another river from the high mountains. From that point, the joined river is called the Ganga. It leaves the mountains at Rishikesh and Haridwar and spreads out onto the plains. In 1968, the Beatles stayed at an ashram in Rishikesh, on its banks.

A glacier gives the Ganga a steady trickle, even in the dry months. But the big flows come from the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. From June to September, rain falls across the whole basin, an area covering about a quarter of India. Streams swell into rivers, and rivers rush to join the Ganga.

The Yamuna joins at Prayagraj. Big rivers from Nepal, such as the Ghaghara, Gandak and Kosi, join further east. The Kosi carries so much sand and shifts its course so often that it has been called the "Sorrow of Bihar". By the time the Ganga reaches [[@bangladesh|Bangladesh]], it is several kilometres wide in places.

The Ganga is home to the Ganges river dolphin, India's national aquatic animal. It is nearly blind and lives in muddy water, so it finds its way and its food by sound, sending out clicks and listening for echoes, a skill called [[echolocation|echolocation]].

The river also holds the gharial, a crocodile with a long, thin snout made for catching fish, and many kinds of turtles. In the delta, [[@sundarbans-tigers|tigers]] swim between islands in the [[@mangroves|mangroves]].

Hundreds of millions of people live in the Ganga's basin, more than in most countries. They use the river for drinking water, farming, fishing and transport. For many Hindus, the Ganga is a sacred river, and cities such as [[@varanasi|Varanasi]] and Haridwar have stood on its banks for centuries.

All that use has made parts of it badly polluted by sewage and factory waste. In 2014, India launched a large clean-up programme called Namami Gange. Scientists measure the water regularly to track whether it is getting cleaner.

text: A fan makes you feel cooler by moving air across your skin. It doesn't make the air colder. It helps your body lose heat in two ways.

First, your body is usually warmer than the air around it, so it warms a thin layer of air right next to your skin. On a still day that warm layer just sits there, like an invisible blanket. A fan blows it away and replaces it with cooler air.

Second, your skin is often a little damp with [[@sweat|sweat]]. When sweat evaporates, turning from liquid into gas, it carries heat away from your body. Moving air speeds up [[evaporation|evaporation]], so you cool down faster. A breeze of just a few kilometres an hour can make a warm room feel two or three degrees cooler to your body, even though the thermometer doesn't move.

st.reveal: A thermometer doesn't sweat, so the moving air can't cool it the way it cools you. The fan's motor also gives off a little heat. The fan cools people, not rooms.

sec.h: A machine that cools people, not rooms

sec.t:
Long before electricity, people in hot countries used hand fans made of palm leaves, feathers, paper or silk. In India, big houses, offices and courtrooms had a punkah, a wide cloth or wooden frame hanging from the ceiling. A worker called a punkah-wallah pulled a rope to swing it back and forth, sometimes for hours, often sitting outside the room.

Punkahs were common in the time of the [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] and British rule, especially in the hot plains. It was tiring, poorly paid work. Electric fans slowly replaced it from the early 1900s.

In 1882, Philip Diehl, an engineer in the USA, took a small electric motor he had designed for [[@sewing-machines|sewing machines]] and mounted it on the ceiling with blades. It is usually counted as the first electric ceiling fan. Others soon added lights and better blades. Table fans and pedestal fans followed, and in India the ceiling fan became so common that many homes have one in every room.

Inside every electric fan, a motor uses [[@magnets-how|magnets]] and coils of wire to turn electricity into spinning. Modern fans called BLDC fans use cleverer motors and electronics, and use roughly half the electricity of older ones. Since 2023, every ceiling fan sold in India has needed an energy star label.

Fans work best when the air is dry, because sweat evaporates easily. In the dry heat of a Delhi May afternoon, a fan can make a real difference. In very humid weather, like Mumbai in the [[monsoon|monsoon]], sweat just drips off instead of evaporating, and the fan feels less helpful.

In extreme heat, fans have another limit. If the air is hotter than your skin, about 35 °C, a fan blows hot air onto you and can add heat. In severe [[@heatwaves|heatwaves]], health bodies such as the World Health Organization advise drinking water and staying in the shade. Cool, wet cloths and a cooler place help too. A fan helps most when it's paired with sense.

text: A lightning rod is a pointed metal rod fixed to the highest part of a building. A thick strip or cable of copper or aluminium runs from it down the outside of the building and into the ground, where it connects to metal rods buried in the soil.

If [[@lightning|lightning]] strikes, it hits the rod first because it's the highest point. The huge electric current then rushes down the metal cable into the earth, where it spreads out harmlessly. Without the rod, the current might go through the roof, walls or wiring, starting fires and smashing brick and stone.
The rod doesn't attract lightning from far away, and it doesn't stop strikes. It just makes sure that when they happen, the electricity takes a safe route.

d.try: Work out how far away a storm is from indoors. When you see a flash, count the seconds until you hear the thunder. Divide by three to get the distance in kilometres. If the gap keeps shrinking, the storm is getting closer. If you can hear thunder at all, stay inside.

sec.t:
During a thunderstorm, ice and water inside clouds crash together. This builds up enormous electric charges, like the [[@static-electricity|static electricity]] that makes your hair stand up after you pull off a woolly jumper, but billions of times stronger. When the charge gets big enough, it jumps to the ground as a giant spark.

A bolt can heat the air to about 27,000 °C, hotter than the surface of the Sun. Electricity always looks for the easiest path. Air is a poor conductor, and so are wood, brick and stone. Metal is excellent. A lightning rod offers a metal highway from the sky to the ground, and the current takes it.

There's a popular saying that lightning never strikes the same place twice. It isn't true. Tall, pointed things are hit far more often than flat ground, and they get hit again and again.

The Empire State Building in [[@new-york|New York]] is struck about 20 to 25 times a year, according to the US National Weather Service. Its rod and cables carry each strike safely away. Many temples, church spires, [[minaret|minarets]] and mobile phone towers have lightning protection for the same reason.

India has some of the world's most lightning-filled skies, especially in the weeks before and during the [[@monsoon|monsoon]]. Lightning is one of the most common causes of death from natural events in India, and many victims are farmers working in open fields.

To help, the Ministry of Earth Sciences launched an app called Damini. It warns people when lightning is likely nearby. Experts advise staying indoors during storms, keeping away from tall trees and water, and not lying flat in the open, but crouching low if caught outside. A building with a lightning rod, or a closed car with a metal roof, is one of the safest places to be.

text: A loudspeaker turns an electrical signal back into sound. Inside is a cone, often made of paper or plastic, with a coil of wire glued to its back. The coil sits in the gap of a strong magnet.

When the music signal flows through the coil, the coil becomes a magnet too, and it is pushed and pulled by the fixed magnet. The coil jerks back and forth, and the cone moves with it, pushing on the air in front. Those pushes travel out as [[@sound-travel|sound waves]] and reach your ears. A low note makes the cone move slowly. A high note makes it shiver very fast.

st.prompt: Why can't a phone speaker make deep, booming bass notes well?

options.t: Its cone is too small to push enough air for low notes
Phones are not allowed to play bass
Low notes need more batteries than phones have

st.reveal: Low notes are slow, long waves, and making them loud means shoving a lot of air. A tiny phone speaker can only move a tiny amount. That's why concert speakers for bass have cones as wide as a car tyre.

d.try: Lay a small speaker or phone face up, cover it with a sheet of cling film, and sprinkle a few grains of rice on top. Play music with a strong beat at medium volume. Watch the grains dance on the low notes, and feel the speaker with your fingertip.
myth: The bigger the speaker, the louder it is.

sec.t:
Wire carrying electricity acts like a weak magnet. Wind the wire into a coil and the effect gets stronger. Put that coil near a permanent [[@magnets-how|magnet]], and the two push or pull each other depending on which way the current flows.

A music signal is a current that keeps changing direction, many times every second, in exactly the pattern of the original sound. So the coil keeps being shoved forward and dragged back in the same pattern. A soft rubbery ring around the cone, called the surround, lets it move freely and pulls it back to the middle.

Early gramophones made sound without electricity. A needle shook a small [[diaphragm|diaphragm]], and a big flared horn helped the sound spread. In 1925, two engineers at the General Electric company in the USA, Chester Rice and Edward Kellogg, developed the moving-coil loudspeaker. Their basic design, a coil, a magnet and a cone, is still used in most speakers a century later.

Speakers soon filled radios, cinemas and stadiums. Public address systems let one voice reach a whole crowd, whether at a political rally, a cricket ground or a railway platform announcing your train.

Phones and earbuds have speakers smaller than a fingernail. To sound good, they rely on tricks. Earbuds sit right next to your eardrum, so a tiny movement is enough. Phone makers use software to boost certain notes and fool your brain into hearing deeper bass than the speaker really makes.

[[@noise-cancelling|Noise-cancelling]] headphones go further. A microphone listens to the hum around you, and the speaker plays the exact opposite wave. When the two meet, they cancel each other out, and the noise seems to fade.

A [[@microphones|microphone]] and a speaker are mirror images. In a speaker, current moves the coil and the coil moves air. In a dynamic microphone, air moves the coil and the coil makes current. Some intercoms and walkie-talkies use the same part for both jobs.

Speakers can be very loud, and very loud sound can damage your hearing over time. Loudness is measured in [[decibel|decibels]]. In India, the Noise Pollution Rules of 2000 limit loudspeakers in public places at night, between 10 pm and 6 am, with a few exceptions. A good rule for earbuds is that if someone next to you can hear your music, it is probably too loud for your [[@ears-hear|ears]].

text: अमृता शेरगिल (1913–1941) एक चित्रकार थीं, जिन्हें अक्सर आधुनिक भारतीय कला की नींव रखने वालों में गिना जाता है। उनके पिता [[@punjab|पंजाब]] के एक सिख विद्वान थे और माँ हंगरी की एक गायिका। उनका जन्म बुडापेस्ट में हुआ, उन्होंने [[@paris|पेरिस]] में कला सीखी, और फिर अपनी ज़िंदगी और अपनी कला के लिए भारत को चुना।

उनके चित्रों में आम भारतीय लोग दिखते हैं, ख़ासकर औरतें, जिनके चेहरे शांत और गंभीर हैं, और रंग गर्म और मिट्टी जैसे। बड़े होकर उन्होंने बस लगभग दस साल चित्रकारी की, और 28 की उम्र में चल बसीं। फिर भी उनके चित्रों ने बदल दिया कि भारतीय चित्रकार क्या-क्या मुमकिन मानते थे।

sec.t:
अमृता हंगरी और भारत के बीच पली-बढ़ीं। जब वे आठ साल की थीं, उनका परिवार शिमला आ गया, और उन्होंने चित्रकारी सीखना शुरू किया। माँ ने देखा कि वे कितनी प्रतिभाशाली हैं, और उन्हें पढ़ने के लिए यूरोप ले गईं।

किशोर उम्र में वे पेरिस के एकोल दे बोज़ार में दाख़िल हुईं, जो दुनिया के सबसे मशहूर कला विद्यालयों में से एक है। उन्होंने यूरोप के उस्तादों से सीखा, और पॉल गोगैं जैसे कलाकारों से भी, जिनके गाढ़े, चटक रंग उन्हें बहुत पसंद थे। 1933 में उनके चित्र *यंग गर्ल्स* ने पेरिस सैलॉन नाम की एक बड़ी प्रदर्शनी में स्वर्ण पदक जीता। तब वे मुश्किल से 20 की थीं।

sec.h: भारत को चित्रित करने घर वापसी

sec.t:
1937 में उन्होंने दक्षिण भारत की यात्रा की। उन्होंने प्राचीन [[@ajanta-colours|अजंता के गुफ़ा चित्र]], [[@pallavas|महाबलीपुरम के मंदिर]] और [[@kerala|केरल के भित्तिचित्र]] देखे। दीवारों पर बने इन [[mural|भित्तिचित्रों]] और मूर्तियों ने उन्हें भीतर तक छू लिया, क्योंकि यहाँ एक ऐसी भारतीय परंपरा थी जो यूरोप की किसी भी चीज़ जितनी समृद्ध थी।

इसके बाद उन्होंने तीन मशहूर चित्र बनाए, जिन्हें कभी-कभी उनकी दक्षिण भारतीय [[series|त्रयी]] कहा जाता है: *ब्राइड्स टॉयलेट*, *ब्रह्मचारीज़* और *साउथ इंडियन विलेजर्स गोइंग टू मार्केट*। रंग और गर्म हो गए, आकार ज़्यादा सपाट और सरल। वे पेरिस में सीखी बातों को भारतीय दीवारों पर देखी चीज़ों से मिला रही थीं।

बाद में उन्हें मुग़ल [[dynasty|राजवंश]] के दौर के और पहाड़ी लघुचित्रों से प्रेरणा मिली, और वे छोटी-छोटी आकृतियों और गाढ़े पैटर्न वाले गाँव के दृश्य बनाने लगीं। उन्होंने हंगरी के एक डॉक्टर से शादी की और कुछ समय उत्तर प्रदेश में सराया नाम की एक चीनी जागीर पर रहीं। 1941 में दोनों लाहौर चले गए, जो तब ब्रिटिश भारत का हिस्सा था।

बस कुछ महीनों बाद वे अचानक बीमार पड़ीं और चल बसीं। वे 28 की थीं। इतनी जल्दी चले जाने की वजह से उनके बस लगभग 170 चित्र ही हमें पता हैं।

sec.h: वे आज भी क्यों मायने रखती हैं
sec.t:
उनके जाने के बाद उनकी ख्याति बढ़ती ही गई। 1976 में भारत सरकार ने उनकी कृतियों को राष्ट्रीय कला निधि घोषित किया, यह सुरक्षा बहुत कम कलाकारों को मिली है। उनके ज़्यादातर चित्र अब [[@delhi|नई दिल्ली]] के राष्ट्रीय आधुनिक कला संग्रहालय में हैं, जहाँ लोग उन्हें [[@museums|संग्रहालय]] में देख सकते हैं।

आज नीलामियों में उनके चित्र बहुत ऊँचे दामों में बिकते हैं। उससे भी ज़रूरी बात यह कि उन्होंने बाद के कलाकारों को दिखाया कि उन्हें भारत और बाकी दुनिया में से किसी एक को चुनने की ज़रूरत नहीं। वे औरतों को चित्रित करने वाली एक औरत थीं, उस ज़माने में जब यह कम ही होता था, और उन्होंने उन्हें अपने भीतर की दुनिया वाले असली इंसानों की तरह चित्रित किया।

text: भारत के शास्त्रीय नृत्य पुरानी और खूब साधना से सीखी जाने वाली शैलियाँ हैं, जो पूरे शरीर से कहानी कहती हैं। संगीत, नृत्य और नाटक की राष्ट्रीय अकादमी, संगीत नाटक अकादमी, आठ नृत्यों को मान्यता देती है। ये हैं तमिलनाडु का भरतनाट्यम, उत्तर भारत का कथक, केरल के [[@kathakali|कथकली]] और [[@kuchipudi-mohiniyattam|मोहिनीअट्टम]], आंध्र प्रदेश का कुचिपुड़ी, ओडिशा का [[@odissi|ओडिसी]], मणिपुर का [[@manipuri-dance|मणिपुरी]] और असम का सत्रिया।

हर नृत्य का रूप और संगीत अलग है। पर सबमें एक प्राचीन ग्रंथ, *नाट्यशास्त्र*, की एक बात साझी है: नृत्य सिर्फ़ कदमों का खेल नहीं, उसे भाव दिखाकर दर्शकों का मन छूना चाहिए। नर्तक की आँखें, भौंहें और उँगलियाँ उतनी ही ज़रूरी हैं जितने पैर।

st.reveal: संगीत नाटक अकादमी आठ नृत्य मानती है, उत्तर के कथक से लेकर दक्षिण के मोहिनीअट्टम तक, और पूर्वोत्तर के मणिपुरी और सत्रिया भी। कुछ सरकारी सूचियाँ नौवाँ नृत्य भी जोड़ती हैं, छऊ, जो पूर्वी भारत का मुखौटा नृत्य है।

d.try: दो मुद्राएँ बनाकर देखो। पताका के लिए हथेली सीधी रखो, उँगलियाँ आपस में सटी हों और अँगूठा अंदर मुड़ा हो, झंडे की तरह। अलपद्म के लिए उँगलियाँ खूब फैलाओ और उन्हें थोड़ा मोड़ो, जैसे खिला हुआ कमल। अब बस इन्हीं दो मुद्राओं और अपने चेहरे के भावों से एक छोटी-सी कहानी गढ़ो, और देखो कि दोस्त समझ पाता है या नहीं।

इनकी जड़ें बहुत पुरानी हैं, पर आज मंच पर जो नृत्य दिखते हैं, उन्हें पिछले दो सौ सालों में गढ़ा गया, और कुछ को तो दोबारा खड़ा किया गया। गुरुओं की हर पीढ़ी ने इनमें कुछ न कुछ बदला है।

sec.t:
कहा जाता है कि *नाट्यशास्त्र* भरत मुनि नाम के एक ऋषि ने लिखा, लगभग 200 ईसा पूर्व से 200 ईसवी के बीच किसी समय। ठीक तारीख किसी को नहीं पता, और हो सकता है इसे कई लोगों ने मिलकर लिखा हो। इसमें अभिनय, संगीत, साज-सज्जा, मंच बनाने और नृत्य के बारे में बड़े विस्तार से बताया गया है।

किताब बताती है कि एक प्रस्तुति दर्शकों के मन में *रस* कैसे जगाती है। रस यानी भावना का एक तरह का स्वाद, जैसे प्रेम, साहस, हँसी या डर। इसमें 108 *करण* गिनाए गए हैं, यानी नृत्य की मुख्य मुद्राएँ और चालें। सदियों बाद तमिलनाडु के मंदिरों की दीवारों पर शिल्पकारों ने ये मुद्राएँ पत्थर में उकेरीं, और आज के नर्तक भी इन्हें सीखते हैं।

ये शैलियाँ अलग-अलग जगहों पर पनपीं, अक्सर मंदिरों, राजदरबारों और गाँव के मेलों-त्योहारों से जुड़कर। [[@kerala|केरल]] के कथकली में घेरदार भारी घाघरे, [[@art-kathakali-makeup|हरे रंग से रँगे चेहरे]] और आँखों की ऐसी हरकतें होती हैं जो दूर बैठे दर्शक को भी दिख जाएँ। परंपरा से इसकी प्रस्तुति पूरी रात चलती थी।

ओडिशा के ओडिसी में शरीर [[@sculpture|मूर्तियों जैसी]] बल खाती मुद्राओं में ढलता है। ऐसी ही आकृतियाँ [[@konark|कोणार्क के सूर्य मंदिर]] पर उकेरी दिखती हैं। मणिपुरी नृत्य कोमल और बहता हुआ होता है, अक्सर कृष्ण की कथाएँ कहता हुआ। सत्रिया 500 से भी ज़्यादा साल पहले असम के [[monastery|मठों]] में रचा गया, पर सरकारी सूची में यह 2000 में जाकर जुड़ा।

1800 के दशक के आखिर और 1900 की शुरुआत में इनमें से कई परंपराएँ मुश्किल में थीं। राजघरानों के [[patron|संरक्षकों]] की दौलत चली गई, और कुछ समाज-सुधारकों ने मंदिरों में होने वाले नृत्य का विरोध किया। आज़ादी के आसपास के दशकों में कुछ राज्यों ने मंदिरों में नृत्य के खिलाफ़ कानून भी बना दिए।

नर्तकों और गुरुओं ने इस कला को ज़िंदा रखने के लिए संघर्ष किया। 1930 में कवि वल्लतोल नारायण मेनन ने कथकली सिखाने के लिए केरल कलामंडलम की स्थापना की। 1936 में रुक्मिणी देवी अरुंडेल ने [[@bharatanatyam|भरतनाट्यम]] के नर्तक तैयार करने के लिए चेन्नई में कलाक्षेत्र शुरू किया। इस नए जन्म में पुरानी परंपराएँ कितनी बदलीं, और कौन लोग पीछे छूट गए, इस पर लोग आज भी बहस करते हैं।

sec.h: कहानियाँ जो कभी पुरानी नहीं होतीं
sec.t:
बहुत-से नृत्य अपनी कहानियाँ *रामायण* और [[@mahabharata|महाभारत]] जैसे [[epic|महाकाव्यों]] से लेते हैं, और कृष्ण व शिव जैसे देवताओं पर लिखी कविताओं से। कुछ नृत्य प्रकृति, ऋतुओं या प्रेम की बात करते हैं।

आज भारत, अमेरिका और दुनिया भर में बच्चे ये नृत्य सीखते हैं। अमेरिका के शहरों में शनिवार को किसी स्कूल के हॉल में किसी नन्ही नर्तकी का *अरंगेट्रम* होना आम बात है। यह उसकी पहली पूरी एकल प्रस्तुति होती है। जो कला कभी सिर्फ़ मंदिरों और महलों में सिखाई जाती थी, वह आज घुँघरुओं से भरे सूटकेसों में दुनिया घूम रही है।

text: Every five years, India elects the 543 members of the Lok Sabha, the lower house of [[@lok-sabha-rajya-sabha|Parliament]]. The party or group that wins most seats forms the government. In 2024, about 98 crore people were registered to vote, more than the entire populations of the USA and the European Union put together.

The independent [[@election-commission|Election Commission]] runs the whole thing. In 2024 it set up about 10.5 lakh polling stations. Voting took place in seven phases spread across six weeks, from 19 April to 1 June. All the votes were counted on a single day, 4 June. About 64.6 crore people voted.

options.t: One
About 50
About 500

st.reveal: A priest who looks after a temple in the forest is the only registered voter there. A team of officials treks in with a voting machine at every general election so he doesn't have to travel far. Lions live in the same forest.

myth: India's voting machines are connected to the internet, so results arrive the moment people vote.

Each machine runs on its own battery and has no internet or wireless link. Votes stay stored inside until counting day, when the machines are opened in front of candidates' agents and the totals are read out one by one.
facts: One of the highest polling stations

sec.t:
Holding everything on one day would need too many police and officials at once. So the country votes in phases, region by region, and security forces move from place to place between them.

The summer timing is a problem. Temperatures in parts of north India reached well over 45 °C during the 2024 polls. Booths were told to provide shade, water and first aid. Voters over 85 and people with disabilities could, for the first time in a general election, choose to vote from home.

India first tried electronic voting machines in 1982 and has used them in every booth across the country since 2004. A machine is a small box with a button beside each candidate's name and symbol. Symbols matter because millions of voters cannot read well. A lotus, a hand, a bicycle or an elephant can stand for a whole party.

Since 2019, every machine has a printer attached. When you press a button, a slip with your candidate's name and symbol appears behind glass for seven seconds, then drops into a sealed box. Some critics have argued for a full return to paper ballots. In April 2024, India's Supreme Court rejected that demand.

Before leaving, each voter gets a line of purple ink painted on the left forefinger. It cannot be washed off for days, so nobody can vote twice. The ink has come from the same company in Mysuru since 1962.

On 4 June 2024, counting began at 8 in the morning in hundreds of halls across the country. Each machine was opened, read and checked in front of agents from the parties. By evening, television screens were full of maps changing colour seat by seat, and most results were clear by night.

India's first general election, in 1951–52, took about four months and used a separate ballot box for every candidate. Many people then were voting for the first time in their lives. The scale today is far bigger, but the idea is the one written into the Constitution: every adult citizen, rich or poor, gets one vote of equal weight.

In the [[@elections-usa|USA]], elections work differently. Each state sets many of its own rules, and no single national body runs the voting the way India's Election Commission does.

text: Economists usually measure an [[economy|economy]] with GDP, short for gross domestic product. It is the total value of everything a country produces in a year, from rice and cars to haircuts and software. In 2025, India's GDP was about 3.9 trillion US dollars, according to IMF estimates published in April 2026. In Indian numbers, that is roughly 345 [[@lakh-crore|lakh crore]] rupees.

That places India among the six largest economies in the world, after the USA, China, Germany, Japan and the UK. The order shifts from year to year, partly because of exchange rates. If you adjust for the fact that things cost less in India, its economy is the third largest. But India also has about 1.4 billion people, so the average income per person is still modest.

sec.t:
Divide India's GDP by its population and each person gets less than 3,000 dollars a year. In the USA, the figure is well over 80,000 dollars. Averages also hide differences. Some Indians are among the richest people on Earth, while millions of families live on very little.

There are big gaps between states too. Goa, Delhi and Karnataka produce far more per person than Bihar or Uttar Pradesh. Cities like Bengaluru, Mumbai and Hyderabad pull in workers from across the country, a bit like Silicon Valley or New York in the [[@usa-economy|US economy]].

About half of India's GDP comes from services: banking, shops, transport, phone companies, hospitals and software. Companies in Bengaluru and Pune write code and run computer systems for customers around the world.

Factories make cars, medicines, steel, clothes and, more and more, smartphones. India is one of the world's biggest makers of generic medicines and [[vaccine|vaccines]]. It is also the world's largest market for motorcycles and scooters, and its factories turn out millions every year. Farming produces less than a fifth of GDP, but it still employed about 43% of workers in 2025. That gap is one reason many farm families earn little.

Money also flows in from Indians abroad. Millions of Indians work in the Gulf, the USA, the UK and elsewhere, and many send money home to their families. India receives more of these payments, called remittances, than any other country: about 129 billion dollars in 2024, by World Bank estimates. For some families in Kerala or Punjab, that money pays for school fees and new homes.

{{story:upi-payments}}

At independence in 1947, India was poor and mostly rural. For decades the government controlled much of the economy, with licences needed to open or expand a factory. Growth was slow. The [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]] of the 1960s and 1970s helped India grow enough grain to feed itself.

In 1991 India faced a crisis and nearly ran out of money to pay for [[import|imports]]. The government cut red tape, lowered import taxes and welcomed foreign companies. Those [[@economic-reforms-1991|1991 reforms]] set off decades of faster growth. More recently, cheap mobile data and instant payments through apps like UPI have brought millions of people into the digital economy.

In 2025, many reports said India had passed Japan to become the fourth-largest economy. Then, in April 2026, the IMF's new figures put it sixth. Nothing had shrunk. The rupee had weakened against the dollar, so the same economy looked smaller when converted. India had also updated how it measures GDP, which lowered some past figures.

The IMF expects India to climb back up in the next few years, since it is growing faster than most large economies. Rankings make good headlines. For most families, though, what matters more is whether jobs, wages and prices are moving the right way.

text: A farmer's day in India usually starts before sunrise. There are cows or buffaloes to milk, animals to feed and fields to check. Then come the jobs of the season: ploughing, sowing, weeding, watering or harvesting. Many farmers work until dark, with a break in the hottest part of the afternoon.

India has around 14 crore farm holdings, most of them small. About 43% of India's workers earn their living mainly from farming. Their lives follow the [[monsoon|monsoon]], the market and the soil, and no two days are quite the same.

st.reveal: About 43% of India's workers were in agriculture in 2025. In the USA it is under 2%, because farms there are much bigger and use more machines.

myth: Farmers only work at harvest time and rest the rest of the year.
Farm work never really stops. Between ploughing, sowing, weeding, watering, caring for animals, fixing tools and selling crops, most farmers work every day of the year.

sec.t:
Many farming families are up by 4 or 5 in the morning. Milking comes first, because cows need milking at regular times. The milk is carried to a village dairy [[cooperative|cooperative]] or sold to neighbours. Thanks to the [[@white-revolution|White Revolution]], India now produces more milk than any other country, much of it from small farms with just two or three animals.

Next, someone takes the animals out to graze or brings in fodder. Children often help before school, carrying grass or water. Breakfast might be roti with a bit of jaggery and chai, or leftover rice with curd.

In the hot months, many farmers work early and late and rest at midday, when temperatures in north India can pass 45 °C. Evening brings more chores: bringing animals home, cutting fodder for tomorrow and checking the water channels.

The average Indian farm is about 1 hectare, a little bigger than a football field. In the USA, the average farm is close to 185 hectares, more than 170 times bigger. American farms use giant tractors and combine harvesters. Many Indian farmers still use bullocks, small tractors hired by the hour, or their own hands.

On a small farm, every family member often helps. Women do a large share of the work, from sowing and weeding to harvesting and caring for animals, yet they own only a small share of farmland. Some families also run a small side business, like poultry, beekeeping or a shop, to earn extra money.

When the harvest is in, farmers take crops to a local market called a *mandi*. Prices can rise or fall from week to week. For some crops, the government buys at a fixed minimum support price, which gives farmers a safety net.

Farming is risky. Debts, [[drought|droughts]], pests and falling prices can hit hard. The government gives eligible farmers ₹6,000 a year through a scheme called PM-KISAN, and offers crop insurance. Farmers also form cooperatives so they can buy seeds and sell crops together.

Modern tools are spreading. Some farmers use drones to spray crops, soil tests to choose [[fertiliser|fertiliser]] and apps to check prices before going to market. These are part of [[@smart-farming|smart farming]]. India learnt in the 1960s how better seeds and water could change everything, during the [[@green-revolution|Green Revolution]]. And the food on your plate tonight, from rice to dal, has travelled a long road from a farmer's field, a journey told in [[@farm-to-plate|farm to plate]].

text: Infinity means without end. However high you count, you can always add one more. The counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on never stop, so we say there are infinitely many of them. The symbol for infinity, ∞, looks like an 8 lying on its side.

Infinity is not an ordinary number like 7 or a crore. You cannot reach it, and adding one to it does not make it bigger. Instead it is an idea that mathematicians handle with special rules. Some of those rules are very surprising, such as the discovery that some infinities are larger than others.

st.prompt: A hotel has endless rooms, numbered 1, 2, 3 and on forever. Every room is full. A new guest arrives. Can the hotel fit them in?

options.t: Yes, if every guest moves up one room
No, the hotel is full

st.reveal: The guest in room 1 moves to room 2, the guest in room 2 moves to room 3, and so on forever. Because there is no last room, nobody is left without a bed, and room 1 is now free. This puzzle, from the German mathematician David Hilbert, shows that infinity does not behave like a big number.

Gamow G. (1947) One Two Three... Infinity. Viking Press.

d.try: Hold two hand mirrors facing each other, a little apart, with a small toy between them. Look over the top of one mirror. You will see a tunnel of toys getting smaller and smaller. myth: Infinity is the biggest number there is.

Infinity is not a number you can reach by counting. It is the idea of something without end. Mathematicians have also shown that there are different sizes of infinity, so there is no single "biggest" one.
facts: ∞, first used by John Wallis in 1655

sec.t:
No matter how [[@big-numbers|big a number]] you name, a trillion, [[@large-numbers-names|a googol]] or a googolplex, there is always a bigger one. Just add 1, or double it. That is the simplest kind of infinity. It is also why pi's digits can go on forever without repeating.

People have puzzled over infinity for thousands of years. Around 450 BCE, the Greek thinker [[@paradoxes|Zeno]] argued that a fast runner could never catch a slow tortoise with a head start. Each time the runner reaches where the tortoise was, it has moved on a little. Mathematicians later explained that an endless list of ever-smaller steps can add up to a finite distance, so the runner wins.

Ancient Indian thinkers wrote about infinity too. Jain mathematicians sorted numbers into countable, uncountable and infinite, and even described different kinds of infinity. A famous verse in the Isha Upanishad says that when the whole is taken from the whole, the whole remains.

sec.h: The hotel that is never full

sec.t:
In the 1870s and 1890s, the German mathematician Georg Cantor proved something that shocked many people. He showed you cannot match every point on a line, including all the [[@decimals|decimals]], one-to-one with the counting numbers. There are always points left over. So the infinity of points on a line is bigger than the infinity of counting numbers.

Some leading mathematicians of his day rejected his ideas. Today they are a basic part of maths. Cantor went on to show there is no largest infinity at all. For every infinity, there is a bigger one.

You can glimpse infinity in two [[@mirrors|mirrors]] facing each other, which make an endless tunnel of reflections. [[@fractals|Fractals]], shapes like [[@snowflake-six|snowflakes]] and coastlines, show more detail the closer you zoom in, in theory forever.

Whether space itself goes on forever is still an open question. [[astronomer|Astronomers]] can see only a part of the universe, containing hundreds of billions of [[@galaxies|galaxies]], because light from further away has not had time to reach us. Beyond that edge, nobody knows if the universe ends or carries on without limit.

text: Sesame Street is an American children's TV show that began in 1969. It mixes puppets, cartoons, songs and real people on a city street to teach young children letters, numbers, kindness and much more. Its most famous characters are Jim Henson's Muppets, such as Big Bird, Elmo, Cookie Monster, Oscar the Grouch, and Bert and Ernie.

What made it different was the planning. Educators and researchers helped write it and tested episodes on real children. The show has been made in dozens of countries, including India, where it was called Galli Galli Sim Sim.

st.reveal: Researchers showed test episodes to groups of young children and noted when they looked away. Scenes that lost children's attention were changed or cut. Testing like this continued throughout the show's history.

In the 2000s Cookie Monster began singing that cookies are a "sometimes food", which started the rumour. He still eats cookies, just alongside fruit and vegetables.

sec.t:
In 1966, a TV producer named Joan Ganz Cooney and a psychologist named Lloyd Morrisett asked a simple question. Young children already loved television and could sing advertising jingles. Could TV teach them something useful, especially children from poorer families who couldn't go to preschool?

Cooney studied the idea and set up a new organisation, the Children's Television Workshop, now called Sesame Workshop. The first episode aired on 10 November 1969.

Jim Henson and his team made the Muppets, a cross between a marionette and a hand [[@puppetry|puppet]]. Big Bird is a performer inside a giant yellow costume, while Elmo and Cookie Monster are operated from below the camera's view.

Each Muppet was designed to show a type of child. Elmo is a curious three-year-old. Oscar the Grouch shows that it's all right to feel grumpy. Cookie Monster can't control himself around cookies, which makes his lessons about patience funny.

In 2006, an Indian version called Galli Galli Sim Sim began, made with Indian partners and shown on TV channels including Pogo and Doordarshan. Its stories were set in Indian neighbourhoods and spoke in Hindi.

Its Muppets included Chamki, a five-year-old girl who loves school, and Boombah, a big friendly lion who loves food. The show focused on things like going to school, washing hands, and treating girls and boys equally. Local versions have also been made in Mexico, South Africa, Bangladesh, Afghanistan and many other places.

Researchers have studied Sesame Street for decades. Several studies found that children who watched it learned more letters and numbers before starting school. One 2015 study looked at the 1970s, when some American areas could receive the show easily and others couldn't. Children in the areas with good reception did better in their early school years.

The show also tackled harder subjects, like divorce, illness and disaster, and used careful scripts to help children cope. Its research team helped show how young children's [[@brain-development|brains]] learn through repetition and play.

Sesame Street keeps adding Muppets to reflect real children. In 2017 it introduced Julia, a Muppet with autism, created with advice from autistic people and their families. Other new characters have been [[refugee|refugees]] or have a parent in prison.

After more than fifty years, the show still opens on the same street. Its songs about the [[@alphabet-history|alphabet]], counting and friendship have been sung by millions of children, many of whom now watch with their own kids.

text: तुम्हारी [[@immune-system|प्रतिरक्षा प्रणाली]] का काम ख़तरनाक कीटाणुओं पर हमला करना है। जिन लोगों को एलर्जी होती है, उनमें यह किसी बेकसूर चीज़ को भी ख़तरा समझ बैठती है। ऐसी चीज़ को [[allergen|एलर्जन]] कहते हैं। यह पराग हो सकता है, [[@gross-dust-mites|घर की धूल]], बिल्ली, मूँगफली या मधुमक्खी का डंक।

पहली बार शरीर चुपचाप उसके ख़िलाफ़ [[antibody|एंटीबॉडी]] बना लेता है। ये तुम्हारी त्वचा, नाक, [[@lungs-breathe|फेफड़ों]] और पेट की ख़ास कोशिकाओं से चिपक जाती हैं। अगली बार जब वह बेकसूर चीज़ आती है, तो ये कोशिकाएँ फट पड़ती हैं और [[histamine|हिस्टामिन]] नाम का रसायन छोड़ती हैं। हिस्टामिन से ख़ून की नलियाँ रिसने लगती हैं, त्वचा में खुजली होती है और नाक बहने लगती है। इसीलिए एलर्जी ऐसी लग सकती है जैसे कुछ ही मिनटों में ज़ुकाम हो गया हो।

sec.t:
सबसे आम एलर्जी हे फ़ीवर है। बहुत से पेड़, घास और खरपतवार दूसरे पौधों तक पहुँचने के लिए हवा में [[pollen|पराग]] के बादल छोड़ते हैं, ठीक वैसे जैसे कुछ पौधे [[@seeds-fly|बीज उड़ाकर]] भेजते हैं। काफ़ी पराग साँस में चला जाए, तो एलर्जी वाली नाक बहने लगती है।

इंग्लैंड के डॉक्टर जॉन बॉस्टॉक ने 1819 में अपनी ही गर्मियों वाली छींकों और आँखों की खुजली का हाल लिखा। चार्ल्स ब्लैकली को भी यही परेशानी थी। 1873 में उन्होंने अपनी त्वचा पर पराग रगड़ा, उसे सूजते देखा, और साबित कर दिया कि असली दोषी पराग है। भारत में तेज़ी से फैलने वाली एक खरपतवार, पार्थेनियम या गाजर घास (जिसे कांग्रेस घास भी कहते हैं), का पराग एलर्जी की एक जानी-मानी वजह है। अमेरिका में रैगवीड नाम की खरपतवार गर्मियों के आख़िर में सबसे बड़ी परेशानी है, और उसका एक पौधा एक अरब तक पराग कण छोड़ सकता है। पराग की मात्रा आमतौर पर गर्म, सूखे, हवादार दिनों में सबसे ज़्यादा होती है और बारिश से हवा धुलने के बाद घट जाती है।

बहुत से देशों में पिछले सौ सालों में एलर्जी ज़्यादा आम होती लगती है। वैज्ञानिक इसकी वजह पर पूरी तरह सहमत नहीं हैं।

एक विचार, जिसे अक्सर स्वच्छता [[hypothesis|परिकल्पना]] कहते हैं, कहता है कि जो बच्चे कम कीटाणुओं, जानवरों और बाहर की मिट्टी के बीच बड़े होते हैं, उनकी प्रतिरक्षा प्रणाली शायद कम अच्छी तरह प्रशिक्षित होती है। खेतों में पले बच्चों को सच में कम एलर्जी होती लगती है। बहुत से वैज्ञानिक अब मानते हैं कि बात मिट्टी से ज़्यादा तरह-तरह के [[@microbes-friendly|दोस्त सूक्ष्मजीवों]] से मिलने की है। प्रदूषण, खान-पान और जीन भी शायद अपनी भूमिका निभाते हैं।

सालों तक अमेरिका और ब्रिटेन में माँ-बाप से कहा जाता रहा कि जिन बच्चों को एलर्जी हो सकती है, उन्हें मूँगफली से दूर रखें। फिर 2015 में लंदन के एक बड़े अध्ययन में पाया गया कि डॉक्टर की देखरेख में जल्दी मूँगफली वाली चीज़ें खिलाने से ख़तरे वाले शिशुओं में मूँगफली की एलर्जी की संभावना बहुत घट गई।

तब से कई देशों में सलाह बदल गई है। डॉक्टर त्वचा में नन्ही-नन्ही चुभन देकर एलर्जी की जाँच भी कर सकते हैं, और कभी-कभी शरीर को धीरे-धीरे किसी चीज़ को स्वीकार करना सिखा सकते हैं। एलर्जी अक्सर परिवारों में चलती है, और कुछ बच्चों की एलर्जी बड़े होने के साथ चली जाती है। अगर तुम्हें लगे कि तुम्हें किसी चीज़ से एलर्जी है, तो माँ-बाप और डॉक्टर को बताओ।

text: माँसपेशी लंबी, पतली [[cell|कोशिकाओं]] का एक गुच्छा है, जिन्हें रेशे कहते हैं। जब दिमाग किसी [[nerve|नस]] से संदेश भेजता है, तो ये रेशे छोटे हो जाते हैं। माँसपेशी सिकुड़ती है, तो जिस चीज़ से जुड़ी है उसे खींच लेती है।

चलने-फिरने में काम आने वाली ज़्यादातर माँसपेशियाँ मज़बूत डोरियों से [[@bones|हड्डियों]] से जुड़ी होती हैं, जिन्हें [[tendon|टेंडन]] कहते हैं। जब माँसपेशी हड्डी को खींचती है, तो हड्डी किसी जोड़ पर घूम जाती है, जैसे दरवाज़ा अपने कब्ज़े पर। माँसपेशियाँ सिर्फ़ खींच सकती हैं, इसलिए वे जोड़ियों में होती हैं। एक हड्डी को एक तरफ़ खींचती है, और उसकी साथी उसे वापस।
तुम्हारे पास ऐसी 600 से ज़्यादा माँसपेशियाँ हैं, और सिर्फ़ खड़े होने में ही तुम दर्जनों इस्तेमाल करते हो।

sec.t:
*कंकाल वाली माँसपेशियाँ* हड्डियों को हिलाती हैं। जब तुम चाहो, तब तुम इन्हें चलाते हो, इसीलिए तुम हाथ हिला सकते हो या [[@football-world|फ़ुटबॉल]] को किक मार सकते हो।

*चिकनी माँसपेशियाँ* पेट, आँतों और खून की नलियों की दीवारों में होती हैं। ये खाने को आगे धकेलती हैं और खून की नलियों को सँकरा या चौड़ा करती हैं, बिना तुम्हारे कभी सोचे।

*दिल की माँसपेशी* सिर्फ़ [[@heart-beat|दिल]] में मिलती है। यह दिन में लगभग 1 लाख बार सिकुड़ती है, पूरी ज़िंदगी, और इसे कभी आराम की ज़रूरत नहीं पड़ती।

कोहनी एक [[@lever-lift|लीवर]] की तरह काम करती है। बाइसेप्स कोहनी के ठीक नीचे, जोड़ के पास जुड़ी होती है। इसका मतलब है कि उसे ज़ोर से खींचना पड़ता है, पर ज़रा-सा सिकुड़ने पर ही हाथ तेज़ी से दूर तक घूम जाता है। वह ताकत के बदले रफ़्तार लेती है, जो गेंद फेंकने में बड़े काम की है।

सबसे बड़ी माँसपेशी कूल्हों की ग्लूटियस मैक्सिमस है। यह तुम्हें सीधा खड़ा रखती है और चढ़ने व दौड़ने में ज़ोर लगाती है। सबसे छोटी, स्टेपीडियस, कान में होती है और बस लगभग एक मिलीमीटर लंबी है। तेज़ आवाज़ आने पर यह कस जाती है, ताकि तुम्हारी [[@ears-hear|सुनने की ताकत]] बची रहे।

आँखें घुमाने वाली माँसपेशियाँ सबसे व्यस्त माँसपेशियों में हैं। हर आँख को छह छोटी माँसपेशियाँ थामे रहती हैं और हर दिशा में घुमाती हैं। पढ़ते समय वे एक सेकंड में कई बार ज़रा-ज़रा झटके देती हैं, और तुम्हें पता भी नहीं चलता।

जब तुम [[@body-strength-limit|भारी चीज़ें उठाते हो]], तो समय के साथ माँसपेशियों के रेशे मोटे हो जाते हैं। उनकी गिनती ख़ास नहीं बढ़ती। 2021 में वेटलिफ़्टर मीराबाई चानू ने टोक्यो [[@olympics|ओलंपिक]] में भारत के लिए रजत पदक जीता। उन्होंने दो लिफ़्ट में कुल 202 किलो उठाया, अपने वज़न के चार गुने से भी ज़्यादा। सालों के अभ्यास ने उनकी माँसपेशियों को इतना ज़ोर से खींचने लायक बना दिया था।

माँसपेशियाँ गर्मी भी बनाती हैं। ठंड लगने पर वे तेज़ी से फड़कने लगती हैं, बिना तुम्हें कहीं हिलाए। यही कँपकँपी है, और यह शरीर का ख़ुद को गर्म करने का तरीका है।

इंजीनियर सालों से माँसपेशियों की नकल करने की कोशिश कर रहे हैं। ज़्यादातर [[@robots|रोबोट]] बिजली की मोटरों से चलते हैं, जो खींचने के बजाय घूमती हैं। कुछ नई रोबोटिक "माँसपेशियाँ" खास प्लास्टिक या ऐसी नलियों से बनती हैं जो हवा भरने पर सिकुड़ जाती हैं। यह असली माँसपेशी के काम करने के तरीके के और करीब है।

text: In the spring of 1856, William Henry Perkin, an 18-year-old chemistry student, was working in a home lab in London during his Easter holidays. His teacher had challenged students to make quinine, a medicine for malaria, from chemicals found in coal tar, the gooey waste left when coal was turned into gas.

Perkin's attempt failed. He got a black sludge. But when he cleaned it out with alcohol, the liquid turned a brilliant purple. He tested it on silk, and the colour didn't wash out or fade in the sun. He had made one of the first synthetic dyes, made from chemicals rather than plants or animals. It became known as mauve.

myth: Purple was always a cheap, everyday colour.

For thousands of years, a lasting purple was rare and costly. Tyrian purple from sea snails was so expensive that, in ancient Rome, it was linked to emperors and the rich. Perkin's mauve helped make purple affordable for ordinary people.

sec.t:
[[@mosquito-diseases|Malaria]], spread by mosquitoes, was a huge killer in the 1800s, including in India and other places ruled by Britain. Quinine, from the bark of the South American cinchona tree, could treat it. But the bark was expensive and hard to get.

Chemists knew quinine contained carbon, hydrogen, nitrogen and oxygen. They hoped they could build it from simpler chemicals. Nobody then understood how [[atom|atoms]] were arranged inside [[molecule|molecules]], so Perkin's plan had little chance. Quinine wasn't made in a lab until 1944.

Purple had always been precious. In the ancient Mediterranean, the best purple came from murex sea snails. Each snail gave just a drop of a special gland's fluid, so it took thousands of snails for a single gram of dye. Roman emperors wore it, and for a time ordinary people were barred from wearing the finest purple.

Now anyone could buy purple cloth. Perkin's discovery started a rush to make new colours from coal tar: magenta, aniline blue and many more. Chemistry became an industry, especially in Germany.

sec.h: A shock for India's indigo farmers
sec.t:
The rush to make dyes from chemicals changed India too. For thousands of years, India had dyed cloth with plants, using madder for red and indigo for blue, in [[@textiles-india|textiles]] and [[@block-printing|block prints]] traded worldwide. British planters forced many Indian farmers to grow indigo, often unfairly.

In 1897, the German company BASF began selling synthetic indigo. Within a few decades, natural indigo [[export|exports]] collapsed. Many planters left, though in Champaran in Bihar the struggle of indigo farmers continued, and in 1917 Gandhi took up their cause.

Here's the twist. Perkin failed to make a medicine, but synthetic dyes later led to many. Scientists found that some dyes stained germs but not human cells. The German doctor Paul Ehrlich used that idea to search for "magic bullets" that would attack only germs. His work helped begin modern drug design, a big chapter in the [[@history-of-medicine|history of medicine]].

Perkin became rich, was knighted in 1906 and died in 1907. Each year, the Perkin Medal honours top chemists in the USA, named after the teenager who couldn't make quinine.

text: A computer doesn't think the way you do. It follows instructions, very precisely and very fast.

Deep inside are billions of tiny switches called [[transistor|transistors]]. Each switch can be on or off, which the computer treats as 1 or 0. Everything it handles, whether numbers, letters, music or photos, is stored as long patterns of 1s and 0s, called [[@binary-code|binary]].

The computer's processor takes in these patterns, follows instructions to combine and compare them, and produces new patterns. It does this billions of times a second. Out of all those simple steps come [[@video-games|video games]], maps and messages.

st.prompt: In binary, using only 0 and 1, how would you write the number 5?
st.reveal: In binary, each place is worth double the one to its right, so the places are worth 4, 2 and 1. Five is one 4, no 2 and one 1, so it is written 101. Computers store every number, letter and colour this way.

sec.t:
Think of a [[@light-switch|light switch]]. On or off. Now connect two switches so that a bulb lights only if both are on. That's a simple [[@logic|logic]] gate, called AND. Wire them so the bulb lights if either is on, and you've made an OR gate.

Join a few of these gates and you can add two [[@maths-binary-fingers|binary numbers]]. Join thousands and you can multiply. Join billions and you have a processor. Modern [[@chips-silicon|computer chips]] pack billions of transistors onto a sliver of silicon smaller than a postage stamp, each switch far too small to see.

The processor, or CPU, works in a loop. It fetches an instruction from memory. It decodes it to work out what to do, such as "add these two numbers" or "jump to another instruction". Then it carries it out. Then it fetches the next one.

A clock inside the computer keeps this loop in step, ticking billions of times a second. A processor running at 3 gigahertz ticks 3 billion times every second. Each instruction is tiny, but at that speed even a long task takes only a moment.

Those instructions are written by people as [[@programming|programs]], then translated into [[binary|binary]] the processor can follow.

{{story:binary-code}}

A computer needs a place to keep what it's working on. Its working memory, called RAM, is fast but forgets everything when the power goes off. It's like the top of your desk while you're doing homework.

For things it must keep, like your photos, songs and apps, it uses storage: a flash chip in phones, or a hard disk or solid-state drive in many computers. This is more like a cupboard. It is slower to reach, but it keeps things safe when switched off. Our article on [[@data-storage|data storage]] goes deeper.

Computers also need ways to take in information and show results. A keyboard, mouse, touchscreen, microphone or camera brings information in. A screen, speaker or printer sends it out. Wires and radio signals connect computers to each other and to the [[@internet-how|internet]].

The same basic design runs in a laptop in Bengaluru, a [[@tech-game-consoles|games console]] in Texas and the chip in a [[@washing-machines|washing machine]]. India built its first supercomputer, PARAM 8000, in 1991 at C-DAC in [[@pune|Pune]], joining together many processors to work at once.

A computer is far faster than any person at arithmetic. It doesn't get bored or tired. But it does exactly what it's told, even when the instructions are wrong. A single mistake in a program can make it crash.

That is very different from [[@brain-works|your brain]], which is slower at sums but brilliant at recognising faces, understanding jokes and learning from just a few examples. Your brain's 86 billion [[@nervous-system|nerve cells]] work all at once, in a messy, flexible way. Even the cleverest artificial intelligence today runs on the same simple on-and-off switches as every other computer.

text: Ancient Greece was not one country but hundreds of small city-states, such as Athens, Sparta and Corinth, spread across mainland Greece, the islands and the coasts of the Mediterranean. They shared a language, gods and the [[@oddity-ancient-olympics-weird|Olympic Games]], and often fought each other.

From them we inherited a surprising amount: [[@democracy-athens|democracy]], theatre, the [[@olympics|Olympic Games]] and much of Western [[philosophy|philosophy]]. They also left ideas in maths and science, styles of building still copied today, and thousands of English words, from "telephone" to "dinosaur".

st.prompt: Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes measured the size of Earth. What did he use?

options.t: Shadows cast by the Sun in two different cities
A ship that sailed all the way around the world
Counting the stars on a clear night

st.reveal: At noon on midsummer's day, the Sun was straight overhead in Syene, now Aswan, but cast a small shadow in Alexandria. The angle was about one-fiftieth of a circle. Knowing the distance between the cities, he multiplied by 50 and came close to Earth's true size.

myth: Ancient Greek statues and temples were always plain white marble.

They were painted in bright colours, with patterned clothes, coloured eyes and gilded details. Over thousands of years the paint wore away, and later artists copied the white stone, thinking that was how the Greeks wanted it.

sec.t: In 508 BCE, Athens began a system in which ordinary male citizens met to vote on laws and decisions. They called it *demokratia*, rule by the people. It left out women, enslaved people and foreigners, so only a minority could vote. Even so, the idea that citizens, not a king, should decide has shaped governments from Delhi to Washington.

Greek theatre grew out of festivals for the god Dionysus. Writers such as Sophocles wrote tragedies about heroes and fate, and Aristophanes wrote comedies that mocked politicians. [[@art-masks-world|Actors wore masks]], and huge open-air theatres were built into hillsides. At Epidaurus, a theatre for about 14,000 people still has such good sound that an actor speaking normally on stage can be heard in the top rows.

Philosophers asked big questions: what is a good life, what is the world made of, how can we know anything? [[@socrates|Socrates]] questioned everyone in the marketplace. His student Plato founded a school, and Plato's student Aristotle studied everything from animals to politics. Aristotle later taught a young prince who became Alexander the Great.

Greek temples stood on rows of stone columns, in styles named Doric, Ionic and Corinthian. [[@acropolis|The Parthenon in Athens]], built for the goddess Athena, is the most famous. Its builders bent its lines very slightly so that it would look perfectly straight from below.

Look at the Supreme Court building in Washington, D.C., or many old banks, museums and colleges in India, and you will see Greek-style columns. The Lincoln Memorial is modelled on a Greek temple.

In 326 BCE, Alexander the Great crossed into Punjab and fought King Porus near the Jhelum River. His tired army refused to march further east, and he turned back. Soon after, [[@mauryan-empire|Chandragupta Maurya]] built a great [[empire|empire]] in India. A Greek ambassador, Megasthenes, lived at his court in Pataliputra and wrote a book about India.

Greek kings later ruled parts of north-west India. In the region of Gandhara, sculptors mixed Greek and Indian styles, carving some of the earliest statues of [[@buddha|the Buddha]] with wavy hair and flowing robes.

The Greeks took the [[@words-alphabet-order|alphabet of the Phoenicians]], traders from the eastern Mediterranean, and added letters for vowels. Our own [[@alphabet-history|alphabet]] comes from theirs, through the Romans. Even the word "alphabet" is made of the first two Greek letters, alpha and beta.

text: In the early 1800s, people in Britain drank huge amounts of [[@tea|tea]], and almost all of it came from China. China sold tea, silk and porcelain, but wanted little from Britain except silver. Britain did not like watching its silver drain away.

So British traders found something China's people would buy: opium, a drug made from poppies, which is very addictive. When China's government tried to stamp out the trade, Britain went to war, in 1839 and again in 1856. China lost both times, gave up Hong Kong, and was forced to open its ports.

st.reveal: Lin had trenches dug near the coast at Humen. Workers mixed the opium with salt and lime until it broke down, then flushed it into the sea. It took more than three weeks.

sec.h: The tea, silver and opium triangle
sec.t:
The opium came mostly from British-ruled India. The [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] controlled poppy farming in Bengal and Bihar, and farmers often had little choice about growing it. The drug was processed in government factories at Patna and Ghazipur, then auctioned in Calcutta.

Private traders shipped it to the Chinese coast and smuggled it ashore. They were paid in silver, and that silver bought tea for London. By the 1830s, millions of people in China used opium, and the silver was now flowing out of China instead of in. In India, opium became one of the biggest sources of money for the [[colonial|colonial]] government.

To win the race to China, traders built sleek sailing ships called opium clippers, which could beat the [[monsoon|monsoon]] winds that slowed ordinary ships. Huge fortunes were made. British firms such as Jardine Matheson grew rich, and so did merchants in Bombay, who shipped opium grown in central India alongside cotton. Some of the money built Bombay's early hospitals, schools and mansions.

The writer Amitav Ghosh set a trilogy of novels in this world, starting with *Sea of Poppies* (2008). It follows poppy farmers from Bihar, sailors and traders whose lives the drug pulled together.

Britain sent warships. Its steam-powered gunboats and modern cannons easily beat China's older navy, and soldiers from India fought in the British forces. In 1842 China signed the Treaty of Nanjing. It handed Hong Kong Island to Britain, opened five ports to British trade, and paid a large sum of money.

The Second Opium War, from 1856 to 1860, was worse. British and French troops marched on [[@beijing|Beijing]] and burned the Old Summer Palace, a vast park of halls and gardens built by emperors over 150 years. The new [[treaty|treaties]] made the opium trade legal.

In China, these wars mark the start of what is often called the "century of humiliation", when foreign powers carved out pieces of the country. The anger they left behind helped fuel the revolutions that later remade [[@chinese-revolution|modern China]].

Hong Kong grew into a huge port city under British rule. In 1997 it was handed back to China. Meanwhile, the government factory at Ghazipur in Uttar Pradesh still processes opium today, but now it is used to make strong painkilling medicines.

text: Pompeii was a busy Roman town in southern Italy, near the Bay of Naples. In 79 CE, the volcano Mount Vesuvius, about 10 km away, erupted violently. Within about a day, the town was buried under metres of ash and pumice, a light stone full of holes.

Many people escaped, but more than a thousand died there. The ash sealed the town like a time capsule. Houses, paintings, shops, [[@oddity-ancient-graffiti|graffiti]] and even food survived. When digging began in 1748, Pompeii opened a window onto ordinary Roman life that no history book could match.

st.prompt: In the 1860s, an archaeologist at Pompeii found strange hollow spaces in the hardened ash. What were they?

options.t: Shapes left by people and animals whose bodies had long since decayed
Underground storage rooms

sec.t:
Pompeii had perhaps 10,000 to 20,000 people. It had temples, a large amphitheatre for games, public baths, bakeries and a forum, the main square. Rich families had houses with gardens and painted walls. Water arrived through an [[aqueduct|aqueduct]] and ran to public fountains on street corners. Stepping stones crossed the streets so people could keep their feet dry, while carts rolled between them. It was a fairly ordinary town of [[@ancient-rome|ancient Rome]], which is exactly what makes it so valuable.

The people did not know Vesuvius was a [[@volcano|volcano]]. It looked like a green mountain covered in vineyards. There had been a strong earthquake in 62 CE, and some buildings were still being repaired when the eruption came.

Around midday, Vesuvius blasted a column of ash and rock high into the sky. For hours, pumice rained down on Pompeii, piling up on roofs until some collapsed. Many people fled.

Early the next morning, fast-moving clouds of searing hot gas and ash, called pyroclastic flows, swept down the mountain. They reached Pompeii and the nearby seaside town of Herculaneum. People who had stayed behind did not survive.

A teenager named Pliny the Younger watched from Misenum, across the bay, about 30 km away. Years later he described it in two letters. He compared the ash cloud to an umbrella pine tree, rising up on a tall trunk and then spreading out.

His uncle, Pliny the Elder, a famous writer and the commander of the Roman fleet, sailed towards the eruption to help rescue people. He died on the shore. Today, scientists call powerful eruptions like this one "Plinian".

In 1748 diggers began uncovering Pompeii. Early excavators often hunted for treasure. Later, [[archaeologist|archaeologists]] worked more carefully.

They found bakeries with ovens, one still containing a round loaf of [[@wheat-bread|bread]] turned to charcoal. Walls were covered in graffiti: election slogans, jokes and messages like "I was here". There were about 80 counters selling hot food to people who had no kitchen at home, a Roman version of [[@street-food|street food]].

{{story:street-food}}

In the 1860s Giuseppe Fiorelli began making plaster casts from hollows left in the ash, showing people and animals in their last moments. These casts are a reminder that the ruins were once someone's home.

About a third of Pompeii has not yet been excavated. New finds keep appearing. In 2018, a charcoal scribble on a wall, apparently dated mid-October, raised doubts about the traditional August date of the eruption.

Pompeii is now a [[@unesco-sites|UNESCO World Heritage Site]], visited by millions of people each year. Vesuvius is still active. It last erupted in 1944, and hundreds of thousands of people live on its slopes today, one reason scientists watch it constantly. Many [[@volcano-cities|cities around the world]] share that risk.

text: Boston, in the north-eastern US state of Massachusetts, is one of America's oldest cities. It is famous as a birthplace of the [[@american-revolution|American Revolution]], for its great universities, and for its long love of sport. Its old brick streets, harbour and historic buildings make American history feel close.

Nearby Cambridge is home to Harvard, the oldest university in the US, and MIT, one of the world's leading science and engineering universities. Boston also runs the world's oldest annual marathon, has the oldest major-league baseball park still in use, and opened the country's first [[@metro-trains|underground railway]]. Many Americans see it as the city where their country's story began.

st.reveal: Protesters boarded three ships and dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbour. They were angry about a British tax on tea, and about having no say in Parliament, which made the laws.

myth: The Boston Tea Party was a protest against high tea prices.
The Tea Act of 1773 actually made legal tea cheaper. Colonists objected because Britain was taxing them without their consent, and because one company was being given control of the tea trade.

sec.h: A Puritan town on a harbour
sec.t:
In 1630, English Puritans, a strict Protestant group seeking a place to practise their faith, founded Boston on a hilly [[peninsula|peninsula]]. They named it after Boston, a town in Lincolnshire in England, where some of them came from. The town grew fast thanks to its sheltered harbour, fishing and shipbuilding.

The Puritans cared about education, so that people could read the Bible. In 1635 they founded Boston Latin School, the oldest public school in the US that is still running. A year later, in 1636, a college was founded across the river. It was later named Harvard.

Boston has been home to many inventions. In 1876, Alexander Graham Bell, working in Boston, made the first successful [[@telephone-history|telephone]] call to his assistant. In 1897, the city opened the first underground railway in the United States, the Tremont Street Subway, still in use today.

Hospitals and universities in the Boston area have made big medical breakthroughs, including one of the first public demonstrations of [[anaesthesia|anaesthesia]] during surgery, in 1846. Boston Common, which opened in 1634, is often called the oldest public park in the US.

The Boston Marathon was first run in 1897, a year after the first modern Olympic marathon. It is the world's oldest marathon still run every year, held each April on Patriots' Day. In 1967, Kathrine Switzer became the first woman to run it as an officially numbered entrant, even though an official tried to push her off the course.

Boston's baseball team, the Red Sox, plays at Fenway Park, which opened in 1912. Its tall left-field wall, painted green, is nicknamed the Green Monster. The Red Sox went 86 years without winning the [[@baseball-world-series|World Series]], from 1918 to 2004, and when they finally won, the whole city celebrated. Fans still talk about that year the way their great-grandparents talked about the tea in the harbour.

text: Singapore became a garden city on purpose. In the 1960s it was a newly independent island with crowded [[@slums-housing|slums]], polluted rivers and few parks. Its first prime minister, Lee Kuan Yew, believed that a clean, green city would attract business and make people proud of their new country. In 1963 he planted a tree to start a tree-planting campaign. In 1967 the government announced a plan to make Singapore a "Garden City".

Millions of trees and shrubs were planted along roads, over flyovers and between tall apartment blocks. Today about half of Singapore's land is covered in greenery. It now calls itself a "City in Nature".

st.prompt: Singapore is short of land. How has it found more?

options.t: By filling in parts of the sea with sand and rock
By buying islands from Australia
By building floating platforms for whole neighbourhoods

st.reveal: Since the 1960s, Singapore has reclaimed land from the sea, growing its area by about a quarter. Its airport, port and parts of its city centre stand on land that was once sea.

myth: It is against the law to chew gum in Singapore.

Since 1992, Singapore has banned selling and importing most chewing gum, to keep streets and trains clean. Chewing it is not a crime, and gum for health reasons, such as some nicotine gum, can be bought from pharmacies.

sec.t:
Singapore is an island at the tip of the Malay Peninsula, about 140 km north of the [[equator|equator]]. Its land area is only about 735 km², smaller than Mumbai's metropolitan area, yet about 6 million people live there.

Its name comes from the Sanskrit word Simhapura, meaning "lion city". In 1819, Stamford Raffles of the British [[@east-india-company|East India Company]] set up a trading post there. Singapore became a busy port. In 1963 it joined Malaysia, but in 1965 it separated and became an independent country.

Singapore has no large rivers or lakes, so water is a big worry. The country speaks of "Four National Taps". It collects rainwater in [[reservoir|reservoirs]], buys water from Malaysia, removes salt from seawater, and cleans used water so well that it can be drunk again. That [[@water-purify|purified]] water is called NEWater. Much of it goes to factories, which need very pure water.

Singapore's people have Chinese, Malay, Indian and other roots. Its four official languages are English, Malay, [[@chinese-characters|Mandarin]] and Tamil, so Tamil appears on signs and banknotes. Little India is full of temples, spice shops and flower-garland stalls, especially at Deepavali.

Food brings everyone together at [[@people-street-vendors|hawker centres]], open-air food courts with dozens of small stalls. You can eat chicken rice, roti prata, laksa and dosa side by side. In 2020, UNESCO recognised Singapore's hawker culture as part of the world's intangible heritage. It is the city's version of [[@street-food|street food]].

Singapore is known for strict rules. There are fines for littering, and the sale of most [[@chewing-gum|chewing gum]] has been banned since 1992. Supporters say this keeps the city clean and safe. Critics say some laws, including limits on protests and the press, go too far. Either way, visitors usually notice two things first: the heat, and how green everything is.

Because land is scarce, Singapore has filled in parts of the sea to make more. Its area has grown by about a quarter since the 1960s. Changi Airport, built partly on reclaimed land, holds the Jewel, a glass dome with an indoor waterfall about 40 m high, the tallest in the world.

text: A wazwan is a grand Kashmiri feast, served mainly at weddings and big celebrations. It has many courses, mostly of mutton, cooked slowly by specialist chefs called wazas. The grandest feasts are said to have up to 36 dishes, though many have fewer.

Guests sit on the floor in groups of four and share a large copper plate called a trami, heaped with rice. Servers bring one dish after another: kebabs, ribs, meatballs in red gravy, chicken and more. The feast ends with gushtaba, soft meatballs in a white yogurt gravy, followed by a cup of kahwa, a green tea flavoured with saffron and spices.

They boil it for a whole day until it falls apart
They chop it with very sharp knives for hours

st.reveal: Cooks beat the mutton on a flat stone with wooden mallets until it becomes a smooth paste, then shape it into soft balls. It's slow, noisy work, often done the night before a wedding.

sec.t:
Wazwan cooking often starts the evening before a wedding. Cooks set up large copper pots over wood fires outdoors. For dishes like rista and gushtaba, mutton is pounded on a flat stone with wooden mallets until it becomes a smooth paste. The rhythmic thumping of the mallets is a familiar sound before Kashmiri weddings.

The meatballs are shaped by hand and simmered for hours. Fat from the meat is mixed in so they stay soft.

A wazwan follows an order. Early dishes include tabak maaz, ribs simmered in milk and spices, then fried crisp. Seekh kebabs and roasted chicken may follow.

Then come the famous curries. Rista is meatballs in a fiery-looking red gravy. Rogan josh is mutton in a rich red sauce. Its colour comes from mild Kashmiri [[@chillies|chillies]] and the dried flowers of a plant called mawal, not from strong heat. Yakhni is mutton cooked in a yogurt gravy flavoured with fennel and dried mint.

Gushtaba arrives last, the grand finale of the meat courses. Its pale, creamy gravy is a calm ending after so many red dishes.

Wazwan cooking uses whole spices like [[@cardamom-pepper|cardamom]], cloves, cinnamon and black cumin, plus dried ginger powder and fennel. Many dishes use little or no tomato.

Kashmir is famous for [[@saffron|saffron]], grown on the plateaus around Pampore near Srinagar. A few threads flavour the rice in some dishes and the kahwa served at the end. Each saffron flower gives only three red threads, so it's precious.

The wazwan is mainly a tradition of Kashmiri Muslims. Kashmiri Pandits, the Hindu community of the valley, have their own celebrated cooking, which traditionally avoids onion and garlic and uses asafoetida, fennel and dried ginger instead. Their rogan josh is just as famous, made with yogurt for its rich gravy.

Both communities share a love of rice, lotus stem (called nadru), and haak, a leafy green cooked with [[@mustard|mustard]] oil. Despite the troubles Kashmir has faced, food remains a shared pride, and a cup of kahwa is offered to almost every guest.

Sharing a trami matters. Four people eat from one plate, and the host watches to make sure every guest is served. Leftovers are often packed up and taken home in a cloth or container, which is considered polite, not greedy.

Wazwan has spread to restaurants in Srinagar and beyond, and you can now order a small version in Delhi or even abroad. But many Kashmiris say the real thing still needs a wedding, a crowd and a waza who has been up all night by the fire.
